contentObjective: I can go beyond today's lesson: write a number as a product of its prime factors using a factor tree in trickier cases, and explain WHY it works.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

noticeAndWonder.context: Engineers on Station Helios need to break 84 replacement circuit boards into equal shipping crates, and the crates must be built using only prime-numbered groupings. Start splitting 84 into two factors: 84 = 2 × 42. Then 42 = 2 × 21, and 21 = 3 × 7. What do you notice about how each split works, and what do you wonder about how you'll know when the factor tree is finished?
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Trophy Case Display
revealWordProblem.text: The school trophy case has 84 trophies to arrange on shelves. The display designer wants to break 84 down into its prime factors first, then use those primes to decide how many equal-sized groups of trophies she can create. What is the prime factorization of 84, written both as a product of primes and using exponents? Show each step of your factor tree.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: 84 = 2 × 42. Since 42 is not prime, split it: 42 = 2 × 21. Since 21 is not prime, split it: 21 = 3 × 7. Both 3 and 7 are prime, so the tree is done. The prime factorization of 84 is 2 × 2 × 3 × 7, which can be written with exponents as 2² × 3 × 7. Check: 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 = 4 × 3 × 7 = 12 × 7 = 84. Correct.

turnAndTalk.question: Mission Control needs to break the 60 supply crates into prime parts. Is 60 a prime number or a composite number, and how can you tell before you even start the factor tree?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 60 is composite because it has more than two factors.

stems.en: 60 is a ___ number because it has ___.
I can tell before factoring because ___.
stems.es: Puedo saberlo antes de factorizar porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students say 60 is composite because it has more than two factors (it is divisible by numbers other than 1 and 60, such as 2, 3, 5, 6), so it can be broken down.
turnAndTalk.extend: Could Mission Control ever be asked to factor a prime number of crates, like 59? Explain what its factor tree would look like and why.
extendStems: A prime number like 59 ___ because its only factors are ___.

turnAndTalk.question: Look at your factor tree for 60. How did you decide which numbers to break apart first, and how do you know when to stop?
turnAndTalk.kernel: You keep splitting until every branch is a prime number.

stems.en: I knew I was finished when every factor was ___.
stems.es: Supe que terminé cuando cada factor era ___.

stems.en: A prime number is ___, so I cannot break it apart.
stems.es: Un número primo es ___, así que no puedo separarlo.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students explain they keep splitting composite branches and stop only when every leaf is prime, ending with 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
turnAndTalk.extend: Two classmates started 60 as 6 × 10 and 4 × 15. Will they get the same prime factorization? Justify why or why not.
extendStems: They ___ get the same prime factorization because ___.
No matter how I start the tree, I always end with ___ because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: The party planner has 72 balloons. How could the prime factorization of 72 help her find every way to arrange the balloons in equal rows?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Combining the prime factors of 72 builds all of its factors.

stems.en: The prime factorization of 72 is ___, written with exponents as ___.
stems.es: La factorización prima de 72 es ___, escrita con exponentes como ___.

stems.en: She can find all the factors by ___ the prime factors.
stems.es: Puede hallar todos los factores al ___ los factores primos.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students give 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 2³ × 3² and reason that multiplying different combinations of those primes produces all factors (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, 72) and thus all equal-row arrangements.
turnAndTalk.extend: Why does writing the prime factorization with exponents (2³ × 3²) make it easier to count how many factors 72 has than writing it the long way?
extendStems: I can use the exponents to ___ instead of listing every factor by ___.

turnAndTalk.question: How is a prime number different from a composite number, and why can every composite number be written as a product of primes?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Primes are the building blocks that every composite number is made from.

stems.en: A prime number has ___, but a composite number has ___.
stems.es: Un número primo tiene ___, pero un número compuesto tiene ___.

stems.en: Every composite number can be built from primes because ___.
stems.es: Todo número compuesto se puede formar con primos porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students contrast exactly-two-factors (prime) with more-than-two-factors (composite) and explain that primes are the building blocks, so any composite splits into a unique product of primes.
turnAndTalk.extend: Is 1 prime, composite, or neither? Defend your answer using the definition of a prime number.
extendStems: It does not fit the definition of prime because ___.

turnAndTalk.kernel: Keep breaking a number apart until every factor is a prime number you cannot split anymore.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.

vocabulary.definition: A number bigger than 1 that you can only divide by 1 and itself.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un número mayor que 1 que solo se puede dividir entre 1 y sí mismo.
vocabulary.visual: 7 has only two factors: 1 × 7. So 7 is prime.
vocabulary.cloze: A whole number greater than 1 with exactly two factors, 1 and itself, is a ___ number.

examples.why: 9 = 3 × 3, so it has more than two factors.
1 has only one factor, so it is not prime.

vocabulary.definitionVi: Số tự nhiên lớn hơn 1 chỉ có hai ước là 1 và chính nó.
vocabulary.definitionAr: عدد طبيعي أكبر من 1 له عاملان فقط: نفسه والواحد.

vocabulary.definition: A number bigger than 1 that you can divide by more than just 1 and itself.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un número mayor que 1 que se puede dividir entre más números, no solo 1 y sí mismo.
vocabulary.cloze: A whole number greater than 1 that has more than two factors is a ___ number.

examples.why: 15 = 3 × 5, so it has more than two factors.
5 is prime; it has only two factors.
2 is prime; its only factors are 1 and 2.

vocabulary.definitionVi: Một số tự nhiên lớn hơn 1 có nhiều hơn hai ước.
vocabulary.definitionAr: عدد صحيح موجب أكبر من 1 له أكثر من عاملين.

vocabulary.definition: Writing a number as prime numbers multiplied together.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Escribir un número como números primos multiplicados.
vocabulary.termVi: Phân tích nhân tử nguyên tố
vocabulary.definitionVi: Viết một số dưới dạng tích của các số nguyên tố.
vocabulary.definitionAr: كتابة عدد صحيح على شكل حاصل ضرب أعداد أولية فقط.

vocabulary.definition: A number that divides evenly into another number, with no remainder.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un número que divide exactamente a otro número, sin dejar residuo.
vocabulary.cloze: A number that divides evenly into another number is called a ___.

examples.why: 12 ÷ 5 = 2 remainder 2, so 5 does not divide 12 evenly.

vocabulary.definitionVi: Số chia hết cho một số khác mà không có số dư.
vocabulary.definitionAr: عدد يقسم عددًا آخر قسمة تامة بدون باقٍ.

launch.narrative: This is your challenge small group for Lesson 1.1. You've got the basics — now let's push on it: harder cases, a second strategy, and always the question "how do you KNOW?"
launch.contextImage: Space station cargo bay with robots sorting crates into smaller equal groups
noticePrompts: What number are we breaking down into factors?
What's the difference between a factor and a prime factor?
wonderPrompts: How many different ways can we start breaking 60 apart?
Will we always get the same prime factors no matter how we start?

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — What is prime factorization?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Keep breaking a number apart until every factor is a prime number you cannot split anymore. — and you can explain WHY, and predict when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: I want the prime factorization of 60. I start by splitting it: 60 = 6 × 10.
6 is not prime, so I break it: 6 = 2 × 3. Both 2 and 3 are prime, so I stop those branches.
10 is not prime, so I break it: 10 = 2 × 5. Both 2 and 5 are prime, so I stop.
Using exponents, I write it as 2² × 3 × 5. I check: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60. Correct.

weDo.title: Generalize it
lines: Start from what you know: Let's factor 12 together. What is one way to split 12 into two factors? (You might say 3 × 4.)
Now predict: what happens with much bigger numbers, or numbers that share no common factors? Make a prediction, then check it.

lines: Work the challenge problems below. For each one, be ready to justify your answer to a skeptic.
If you finish early: find a second strategy, or a case where it would break.

onLevel.stem: Two students found different factor trees for 60. Student A started with 2 × 30. Student B started with 6 × 10. Which statement is true?
choices: Both get the same prime factorization: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5
Only Student A gets the correct prime factorization
Only Student B gets the correct prime factorization
They will get different prime factorizations
onLevel.explanation: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every composite number has exactly one prime factorization. No matter how you start the factor tree, you always end with 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
choiceFeedback: Try listing the factors again—check each one.
hints: Notice the question isn't asking which START is right — it asks what happens when both finished trees are compared.
Finish BOTH trees yourself: keep splitting every branch down to primes, then compare the two final lists of prime factors.
Student A: 60 = 2 × 30, then 30 = 2 × 15, then 15 = 3 × 5. Now finish Student B's tree from 6 × 10 and compare the prime lists.

onLevel.title: onLevel — Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Find the prime factorization of 45, using exponents

onLevel.correctWork: 45 = 5 × 3 × 3 has one 5 and two 3's — not two 5's. The exponent on a prime factor shows how many times that factor appears, so the correct form is 45 = 3² × 5 (the 5 has no exponent shown because it appears only once).
hints: Count how many times each prime factor actually appears in the factor tree before you write its exponent.
5 only appears once in 45 = 3 × 3 × 5, so its exponent is 1 (usually left off) — not 2.

extending.title: Find Marcus's Mistake
extending.correctWork: 8 = 2 × 4, but 4 is not prime. 4 = 2 × 2, so 8 = 2 × 2 × 2. The correct prime factorization is 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁴ × 3.
hints: Look at Step 4 — is every factor in the answer a prime number?
4 is not prime because 4 = 2 × 2. Marcus needed to keep breaking it down.

extending.prompt: Choose any two-digit composite number. Show TWO different factor trees that both lead to the same prime factorization. Explain why every composite number has only one prime factorization.
extending.sentenceFrame: I chose the number ___. My first factor tree starts with ___ × ___, and my second starts with ___ × ___. Both give the same prime factorization: ___. This happens because ___.
hints: Re-read the task: pick ONE two-digit composite number (like 24, 36, or 40) and build TWO trees with different first splits.
Choose two different starting pairs for your number — for 36 you could start with 4 × 9 or 6 × 6 — and finish both trees to primes.
Say you pick 24: tree one starts 2 × 12, tree two starts 4 × 6. Finish both, list each tree's primes, and explain why the lists match.

extending.label: Write the prime factorization using exponents.
hints: An exponent counts repeats: 2 × 2 × 2 is three 2s, written 2³. The expanded column already lists every prime for you.
Group the identical primes together, count how many of each there are, and write each prime with its count as an exponent.
For 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3: count the 2s first — there are three — so write 2 with that exponent, then count and write the 3s.

optional.stem: The first lock panel shows 90. What is the prime factorization of 90?
optional.explanation: 90 = 2 × 45 = 2 × 9 × 5 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 5. Every factor is prime, so the lock accepts 2 × 3 × 3 × 5.
choiceFeedback: Check if every factor in that product is actually prime.

optional.stem: The second panel needs a number whose prime factorization is 2² × 3². Which number unlocks it?
optional.explanation: 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36, so 36 is the code for this panel.
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.

optional.stem: The final lock asks for the prime factorization of 78 written as a product of primes. Which is correct?
optional.explanation: 78 = 2 × 39 = 2 × 3 × 13. All three factors are prime, so 2 × 3 × 13 unlocks the final panel.
choiceFeedback: Check if every factor in that product is actually prime.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Prime Factorization is stopping the factor tree too soon — leaving a composite number like 4, 6, 8, or 9 in the final answer instead of continuing to split it. For example, writing 20 = 4 × 5 as the prime factorization (4 is composite) instead of finishing with 20 = 2 × 2 × 5. Before you submit, check every number in your final answer: if any factor can still be broken into smaller factors, the tree isn't finished yet.

optionalActivity.name: Factor Tree Code Breaker
optionalActivity.intro: Challenge — prove it: The station's airlock is sealed with a prime-factor code — break each number into primes to unlock all four digits and reboard the ship! Convince a skeptic your answer is right.

connect.scenario: A station gardener is loading 72 seed pods into the greenhouse and wants to build a perfectly rectangular planting grid. Starting from the prime factorization of 72, she combines the prime factors to list every factor of 72 and choose a grid that uses all the pods.
connect.promptQuestion: Starting from its prime factorization, how can the gardener use the factors of 72 to decide which rectangular grids will use all 72 seed pods?
connect.prompt: Because 72 = ___, I can multiply combinations of those prime factors to get factors like ___, so a grid that works is ___ by ___.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — What is the prime factorization of 40?
exitTicket.hint: Think through the problem step by step.
choiceFeedback: 4 and 10 aren't prime — keep splitting until every factor is prime.
8 isn't prime — break it down further into primes.
20 still breaks down — a prime factorization stops only at primes.
hints: A prime factorization keeps going until EVERY factor is prime — factors like 4, 8, 10, and 20 still need splitting.
Build a factor tree for 40 and keep splitting every composite branch until only prime numbers are left at the ends.
Start with 40 = 4 × 10. Split the 4 into 2 × 2, then split the 10 into primes — then collect every prime at the ends of the branches.

smallGroup.label: Challenge
smallGroup.who: Pull students who showed mastery on the formative check and are ready to extend.
moves: Launch the challenge fast — skip the re-teach, they don't need it.
Step back. Let them wrestle; protect the productive struggle.
Ask "How do you know?" and "Can you show it a second way?" more than you explain.
Push for a generalization: when does this hold, and when would it break?
Close by having one student justify a claim to the group.
